name: Default Curriculum
description: The comprehensive learning path from absolute beginner to full-stack developer, aligned with the Edmonds College CIS Web Application Developer Certificate.

exercises.title: Your First HTML Page
exercises.description: Create a basic HTML page with the required document structure.
exercises.instructions:
Every HTML page needs a basic structure to work properly. Create a valid HTML5 page by adding the required elements.

Your page should have:
- A `<!DOCTYPE html>` declaration at the very top
- An `<html>` element with `lang="en"`
- A `<head>` section
- A `<body>` section

This is the skeleton that every web page is built on.
exercises.starterCode:
<!-- Add the DOCTYPE declaration -->

<!-- Add the html element with lang="en" -->

  <!-- Add the head section -->

  <!-- Add the body section -->
hints: Every HTML page starts with a special declaration that tells the browser what version of HTML you are using. What does that declaration look like?
The structure is: DOCTYPE at the top, then an <html> element that contains both a <head> and a <body> section.

exercises.title: Page Title
exercises.description: Add a title to your HTML page that appears in the browser tab.
exercises.instructions:
The `<title>` element sets the text that appears in the browser tab. It must be placed inside the `<head>` section.

Add a `<title>` element inside the `<head>` with the text "My First Page".

Example: When you open a website, the text you see on the browser tab is the page title.
exercises.starterCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <!-- Add a title element with the text "My First Page" -->

  </head>
  <body>
  </body>
</html>
hints: There is a specific HTML element that controls what text appears in the browser tab. Where should it be placed — in the head or the body?
The <title> element goes inside the <head> section. The text you want displayed goes between the opening and closing title tags.

resources.label: W3Schools: HTML Head
resources.description: What goes in the HTML head section

exercises.title: Head and Body
exercises.description: Add a title in the head and a heading in the body of an HTML page.
exercises.instructions:
The `<head>` contains information about the page (like the title). The `<body>` contains what visitors actually see.

Add:
- A `<title>` element inside `<head>` with the text "Hello World"
- An `<h1>` element inside `<body>` with the text "Welcome!"

Remember: The head is for the browser, the body is for the viewer.
exercises.starterCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <!-- Add a title with "Hello World" -->

  </head>
  <body>
    <!-- Add an h1 heading with "Welcome!" -->

  </body>
</html>
hints: The page has two main sections. One holds information the browser uses behind the scenes, and the other holds content the visitor sees on screen.
Use <title> inside <head> for the tab text. Use <h1> inside <body> for the visible heading.

resources.label: MDN: Head element
resources.description: What belongs in the HTML head

exercises.title: Heading Levels
exercises.description: Use heading elements h1 through h3 to create a content hierarchy.
exercises.instructions:
HTML has six levels of headings, from `<h1>` (most important) to `<h6>` (least important). They create a visual and structural hierarchy for your content.

Add the following headings in order:
- An `<h1>` with "Main Title"
- An `<h2>` with "Section Title"
- An `<h3>` with "Subsection Title"

Every page should have exactly one `<h1>`. Use `<h2>` through `<h6>` for subsections.
exercises.starterCode:

<!-- Add an h3 heading with "Subsection Title" -->
hints: HTML provides numbered heading elements for different levels of importance. The number indicates the level in the hierarchy.
Use <h1> for the most important heading, <h2> for the next level, and <h3> for the level after that. Each has an opening and closing tag.

exercises.title: Bold and Italic
exercises.description: Use strong and em elements to add emphasis to text.
exercises.instructions:
HTML provides elements to add emphasis to text:
- `<strong>` makes text **bold** — use it for important content
- `<em>` makes text *italic* — use it for stressed emphasis

Create a paragraph that contains:
- The word "important" wrapped in `<strong>` tags
- The word "really" wrapped in `<em>` tags

The full text should read: "This is really important information."
exercises.starterCode: This is information.
hints: There are two HTML elements that change how text looks and what it means to screen readers. One makes text bold, the other italic.
Wrap the word in the appropriate tag: word for bold, word for italic. These go inside the paragraph.

resources.label: W3Schools: HTML Text Formatting

exercises.title: Line Breaks
exercises.description: Use the br element to create line breaks within a paragraph.
exercises.instructions:
In HTML, pressing Enter in your code does NOT create a new line on the page. To force a line break without starting a new paragraph, use the `

` element is self-closing — it has no closing tag.
hints: HTML ignores extra whitespace and line breaks in your code. There is a special element that forces the browser to move to the next line.

The
element creates a line break. It does not need a closing tag. Place it after each line of text where you want a break.

exercises.title: Preformatted Text
exercises.description: Use pre and code elements to display code snippets on a page.
exercises.instructions:
The `

Create:
- A `

- A `

The `

hints: There are two elements that work together for showing code: one preserves whitespace, and the other marks the content as computer code.
Use <pre> as the outer element to preserve formatting. Nest <code> inside it to mark the text as code.

exercises.title: Unordered List
exercises.description: Create a bulleted list using ul and li elements.
exercises.instructions:
An unordered list displays items with bullet points. It uses two elements:
- `<ul>` — the list container (unordered list)
- `<li>` — each item in the list (list item)

Create an unordered list with three items:
- "Apples"
- "Bananas"
- "Oranges"

Every `<li>` must be inside a `<ul>` to work correctly.
hints: An unordered list needs a container element and individual item elements inside it. What are the HTML tags for these?
The container is <ul> (unordered list). Each item uses <li> (list item) with the text between opening and closing tags.

exercises.title: Ordered List
exercises.description: Create a numbered list using ol and li elements.
exercises.instructions:
An ordered list displays items with numbers. It uses `<ol>` instead of `<ul>`, but the items still use `<li>`.

Create an ordered list with three steps:
1. "Preheat the oven"
2. "Mix the ingredients"
3. "Bake for 30 minutes"

The browser automatically numbers each item for you.
exercises.solution:
1. Preheat the oven
  2. Mix the ingredients
  3. Bake for 30 minutes
hints: A numbered list works just like a bulleted list, but uses a different container element. What tag creates a numbered (ordered) list?
Change <ul> to <ol> for ordered lists. The <li> elements stay the same — the browser handles the numbering automatically.

exercises.title: Grocery List
exercises.description: Build a grocery list with a heading and an unordered list of items.
exercises.instructions:
Practice combining elements by building a grocery list page.

Create:
- An `<h2>` with "Grocery List"
- A `<ul>` with at least 5 items of your choice

Example items: Milk, Bread, Eggs, Butter, Cheese

This combines what you have learned about headings and lists.

testCases.description: At least 5 <li> elements in the list

hints: You need two types of elements: one for the title of the list and one for the list itself with individual items inside.
Use <h2> for the heading. Then create a <ul> with five or more <li> elements, each containing a grocery item.

exercises.title: External Link
exercises.description: Create a link to an external website using the anchor element.
exercises.instructions: Links are created with the `` (anchor) element. The `href` attribute tells the browser where the link goes. Create a link that: - Has the text "Visit Example" - Points to "https://example.com" The format is: `Link Text` The text between the tags is what the user clicks on.
exercises.starterCode:
<!-- Create a link to https://example.com -->
<!-- The link text should say "Visit Example" -->
hints: Links use a special element with an attribute that specifies the destination URL. What element creates a clickable link?
The <a> element creates a link. The href attribute sets the destination. Your text goes between the opening and closing tags.

resources.description: How to create links in HTML

exercises.title: Descriptive Link Text
exercises.description: Write links with meaningful text instead of generic phrases.
exercises.instructions:
Good link text describes where the link goes. Screen readers announce link text to users, so "click here" is unhelpful.

Create two links:
- A link to "https://www.w3schools.com" with the text "W3Schools HTML Tutorial"
- A link to "https://developer.mozilla.org" with the text "MDN Web Docs"

Bad: "Click here to learn HTML"
Good: "Learn HTML at W3Schools"
exercises.starterCode:
<!-- Create a link to W3Schools with descriptive text -->

<!-- Create a link to MDN with descriptive text -->
hints: Each link needs two things: a destination URL and descriptive text. The text should tell the user where the link leads.
Create two <a> elements, each with an href attribute pointing to the correct URL and descriptive text between the tags.

exercises.title: Open in New Tab
exercises.description: Create a link that opens in a new browser tab safely.
exercises.instructions: Sometimes you want a link to open in a new tab so the user does not leave your page. Use the `target` attribute: - `target="_blank"` opens the link in a new tab - `rel="noopener"` should always be added for security when using `_blank` Create a link that: - Points to "https://example.com" - Has the text "Open Example in New Tab" - Opens in a new tab safely Format: `Text`
exercises.starterCode:
<!-- Create a link that opens in a new tab -->
<!-- Include target="_blank" and rel="noopener" -->
exercises.solution: Open Example in New Tab
hints: Links have attributes beyond href that control behavior. What attributes make a link open in a new tab?
Add target="_blank" to open in a new tab. Always pair it with rel="noopener" for security. Both go inside the opening <a> tag.

exercises.title: Email Link
exercises.description: Create a link that opens the user's email program.
exercises.instructions: You can create a link that opens the user's email program by using `mailto:` in the `href` attribute instead of a URL. Create a link that: - Opens an email to "hello@example.com" - Has the text "Send us an email" Format: `Text`
exercises.starterCode: <!-- Create an email link to hello@example.com -->
hints: Links do not always have to point to web pages. The href attribute supports a special protocol for opening email programs.
Instead of https://, use mailto: followed by the email address in the href attribute.

exercises.title: Add an Image
exercises.description: Add an image to a page using the img element with src and alt attributes.
exercises.instructions: Images are added with the `` element. It requires two attributes: - `src` — the image file path or URL - `alt` — a text description of the image (for accessibility) Add an image with: - `src` set to "photo.jpg" - `alt` set to "A beautiful sunset" The `` element is self-closing — it has no closing tag. Format: ``

hints: Images use a self-closing element with two important attributes: one for the file location and one that describes the image in words.
The element needs src for the file path and alt for the description. It does not need a closing tag.

exercises.title: Image Sizing
exercises.description: Set the width and height of an image using HTML attributes.
exercises.instructions: You can control the size of an image using the `width` and `height` attributes directly on the `` element. Add an image with: - `src` set to "banner.jpg" - `alt` set to "Website banner" - `width` set to "600" - `height` set to "200" The values are in pixels. Setting these attributes helps the browser reserve space for the image while the page loads.
exercises.starterCode: <!-- Add an image with width and height attributes -->
hints: Images can have attributes that control their display size on the page. What attributes set the dimensions of an image?
Add width and height attributes to the tag with numeric values (no units needed — they default to pixels).

exercises.title: Linked Image
exercises.description: Wrap an image inside a link to make it clickable.
exercises.instructions: You can make an image clickable by wrapping it inside an `` element. When the user clicks the image, they follow the link. Create a link to "https://example.com" that contains an image: - Image `src`: "logo.png" - Image `alt`: "Example Logo" Format: ``
exercises.starterCode: <!-- Create a link that contains a clickable image -->
hints: You already know how to create links and how to add images. What happens if you put one element inside the other?
Place the element between the opening and closing tags. The image becomes the clickable content of the link.

exercises.title: Simple Table
exercises.description: Create a basic 2-column table with 3 rows of data.
exercises.instructions:
Tables use three main elements:
- `<table>` — the table container
- `<tr>` — a table row
- `<td>` — a table data cell

Create a table with 3 rows and 2 columns:
- Row 1: "Name" and "Age"
- Row 2: "Alex" and "25"
- Row 3: "Sam" and "30"

Each `<td>` goes inside a `<tr>`, and all `<tr>` elements go inside `<table>`.

testCases.description: At least 6 <td> cells exist (3 rows × 2 columns)

hints: Tables are built row by row. Each row contains cells. What elements create a table row and a table cell?
Use <tr> for each row and <td> for each cell within that row. Nest them inside a <table> element.

resources.label: W3Schools: HTML Tables
resources.description: How to create tables in HTML

exercises.title: Table Headers
exercises.description: Use th elements to create bold header cells in a table.
exercises.instructions:
The `<th>` element creates a header cell that is bold and centered by default. Use `<th>` instead of `<td>` for the first row to label your columns.

Create a table with:
- A header row using `<th>` with "Product" and "Price"
- Two data rows using `<td>`:
  - "Coffee" and "$3.00"
  - "Tea" and "$2.50"
exercises.starterCode:
Coffee $3.00
Tea $2.50
hints: Header cells use a different element than regular data cells. What element creates a bold, centered header in a table?
Replace <td> with <th> for the first row to create header cells. Data rows still use <td>.

exercises.title: Table Sections
exercises.description: Organize a table into head, body, and foot sections.
exercises.instructions:
Tables can be divided into three sections for better organization:
- `<thead>` — the header section (column labels)
- `<tbody>` — the body section (data rows)
- `<tfoot>` — the footer section (summary row)

Create a table with:
- `<thead>` containing a row with `<th>` cells: "Item" and "Cost"
- `<tbody>` containing two rows: "Lunch" / "$12" and "Dinner" / "$25"
- `<tfoot>` containing a row: "Total" and "$37"
hints: Tables can be split into logical sections. What three elements divide a table into header, body, and footer areas?
Wrap your header row in <thead>, your data rows in <tbody>, and your summary row in <tfoot>. Each section still uses <tr> and <td>/<th> inside.

resources.description: Table head, body, and foot sections

exercises.title: Text Input
exercises.description: Create a text input with a label using the label and input elements.
exercises.instructions:
Form inputs let users enter data. Every input should have a `<label>` that describes it.

Create:
- A `<label>` with the text "Your Name:" and a `for` attribute set to "name"
- An `<input>` with `type="text"` and `id="name"`

The `for` attribute on the label must match the `id` on the input. This connects them so clicking the label focuses the input.

<!-- Add a label for the input -->

<!-- Add a text input with matching id -->
hints: Form inputs need a visible description and an interactive element where the user types. What two elements work together for this?
Use <label> with a for attribute and <input> with a matching id attribute. The for and id values must be identical.

resources.label: MDN: input element
resources.description: The input element and its types

exercises.title: Form with Button
exercises.description: Build a simple form with a text input and a submit button.
exercises.instructions:
Forms collect user input. A basic form needs:
- A `<form>` container
- An `<input>` for the user to type in
- A `<button>` to submit the form

Create a form with:
- A text input with `id="email"` and `placeholder="Enter your email"`
- A `<button>` with `type="submit"` and the text "Submit"
exercises.starterCode:
<!-- Create a form element -->
<form>
  <!-- Add a text input with placeholder -->

  <!-- Add a submit button -->

</form>
exercises.solution:
<form>
  <input type="text" id="email" placeholder="Enter your email">
  <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>
hints: A form is a container that groups inputs and a button together. What element wraps all form content?
The <form> element contains your inputs and button. The input uses placeholder for hint text, and the button uses type="submit".

exercises.title: Input Types
exercises.description: Use different input types for email, password, and number fields.
exercises.instructions:
The `<input>` element supports many types. Each type changes the behavior:
- `type="email"` — validates email format
- `type="password"` — hides the text as dots
- `type="number"` — only allows numbers

Create three labeled inputs:
- Label "Email:" with an email input (`id="email"`)
- Label "Password:" with a password input (`id="password"`)
- Label "Age:" with a number input (`id="age"`)
exercises.starterCode:
<!-- Email input with label -->
<label for="email">Email:</label>
<input <!-- set type and id -->>

<!-- Password input with label -->
<label for="password">Password:</label>
<input <!-- set type and id -->>

<!-- Number input with label -->
<label for="age">Age:</label>
<input <!-- set type and id -->>

<input type="email" id="email">

<label for="password">Password:</label>
<input type="password" id="password">

<input type="number" id="age">
hints: The input element has a type attribute that changes its behavior. What type values create fields for email, hidden text, and numbers?
Set type="email" for email validation, type="password" to hide text, and type="number" to only allow numeric input.

exercises.title: Placeholder Text
exercises.description: Add placeholder text to inputs that shows hint text before the user types.
exercises.instructions:
The `placeholder` attribute displays gray hint text inside an input. It disappears when the user starts typing.

Create a form with two inputs:
- A text input with `placeholder="Enter your full name"`
- An email input with `placeholder="you@example.com"`

Placeholders help users understand what to type.

  <!-- Email input with email placeholder -->
  <input type="email" <!-- add placeholder -->>
</form>
exercises.solution:
<form>
  <input type="text" placeholder="Enter your full name">
  <input type="email" placeholder="you@example.com">
</form>
hints: There is an input attribute that shows temporary hint text inside the field before the user types anything.
Add placeholder="..." to each input element. The placeholder value is the hint text shown in gray.

exercises.title: Checkboxes and Radio Buttons
exercises.description: Create checkbox and radio button inputs for selections.
exercises.instructions:
Checkboxes let users select multiple options. Radio buttons let users select only one option from a group.

- `type="checkbox"` — can select multiple
- `type="radio"` — can select only one (group them with the same `name`)

Create:
- A checkbox with `id="agree"` and label "I agree to the terms"
- Two radio buttons with `name="color"`: one with `id="red"` labeled "Red", another with `id="blue"` labeled "Blue"

Radio buttons with the same `name` form a group — selecting one deselects the others.
exercises.starterCode:
<!-- Checkbox -->
<input <!-- set type and id -->>
<label for="agree">I agree to the terms</label>

<!-- Radio button group -->
<input <!-- set type, name, and id -->>
<label for="red">Red</label>

<input <!-- set type, name, and id -->>
<label for="blue">Blue</label>
exercises.solution:
<input type="checkbox" id="agree">
<label for="agree">I agree to the terms</label>

<input type="radio" name="color" id="red">
<label for="red">Red</label>

<input type="radio" name="color" id="blue">
<label for="blue">Blue</label>
hints: There are two input types for selection: one allows multiple choices, the other allows only one. What input types are these?
Use type="checkbox" for multi-select and type="radio" for single-select. Radio buttons must share the same name attribute to form a group.

exercises.title: Nav Element
exercises.description: Use the nav element to wrap navigation links on a page.
exercises.instructions:
The `<nav>` element wraps a section of navigation links. It tells browsers and screen readers that these links are the main way to navigate the site.

Create a `<nav>` element containing three links:
